name: Desiccated thyroid (Armour)

angle.text: Desiccated thyroid is used by people who believe fuller T3 and T4 supply improves energy, metabolism and body composition. It is an older hypothyroidism treatment; its use as a slimming or appearance aid is based on anecdote and has not been trialled.

summary: Dried porcine thyroid containing T4 and T3, an older hypothyroidism treatment with no evidence base as a slimming aid.
note: Excess thyroid hormone can cause arrhythmia and heart failure; levothyroxine is guideline-preferred for hypothyroidism.
currentQuick:
Desiccated thyroid is dried animal thyroid gland that supplies both T4 and T3. Armour Thyroid is the best-known brand.
It is prescribed for hypothyroidism, and some people discuss it for weight management; no trials support that use.
How it works: The T4 and T3 in the extract bind thyroid hormone receptors and raise metabolic rate.
Risks and caveats: Batch variability and high T3 peaks are cited concerns. Excess doses can cause arrhythmias, anxiety and heart failure.
deepLead:
Desiccated thyroid extract (DTE) is dried, powdered thyroid gland, usually from pigs, taken orally for hypothyroidism. Armour Thyroid is the best-known brand. It contains both T4 and T3, in a ratio of roughly 4:1 compared with about 11:1 in humans.
It was the main hypothyroidism treatment from the 1890s until synthetic levothyroxine replaced it from the 1960s. The American Association of Clinical Endocrinologists and the Royal College of Physicians recommend levothyroxine over thyroid extract.
Some patients and prescribers prefer DTE, and it is sometimes discussed for weight management. Excessive thyroid hormone doses can cause weight loss but also fever, anxiety, arrhythmias and heart failure. No studies have tested DTE as a slimming treatment in euthyroid people.

name: Medroxyprogesterone acetate

chain: Feminizing changes or reduced hair growth
angle.text: Medroxyprogesterone acetate is used within feminizing hormone therapy and for hirsutism, where altered hormone signaling changes body shape and hair growth. These appearance uses are off-label to its contraceptive role, with limited trial data for them.

summary: A prescription progestin (Depo-Provera) with only peripheral appearance uses, such as feminizing therapy and hirsutism.
note: Boxed warning for bone density loss; WHI trials linked estrogen plus MPA to higher breast cancer and cardiovascular risks.
currentQuick:
MPA is a synthetic progestin used for contraception, menopausal hormone therapy and gynecologic conditions.
Its appearance relevance is limited to feminizing hormone regimens and reports of effects on hair growth.
How it works: It activates progesterone, androgen and glucocorticoid receptors and suppresses GnRH, reducing ovulation and sex hormone levels.
Risks and caveats: Bone density loss, blood clots, menstrual disruption and meningioma have been reported. It is prescription-only.
deepLead:
Medroxyprogesterone acetate (MPA) is a synthetic progestin sold as Depo-Provera (injectable contraceptive, DMPA) and Provera (oral). It was discovered in 1956 and introduced for medical use in the US in 1959.
Its main uses are contraception, menopausal hormone therapy and gynecologic disorders. Appearance-related uses are limited: it is prescribed in feminizing hormone therapy for transgender women, and high-dose DMPA has been reported to treat hirsutism, while decreased scalp hair is a listed side effect.
The injectable label carries a boxed warning for loss of bone mineral density. Large trials of estrogen plus MPA in postmenopausal women found increased risks of breast cancer, coronary disease and stroke.

name: Megestrol acetate

angle.text: Megestrol is a progestin appetite stimulant approved for cancer and AIDS wasting, and it comes up in forum talk about gaining weight on a thin frame. Weight gain is its documented effect in illness; cosmetic or physique use is untested.

summary: A progestin appetite stimulant approved for cancer and AIDS wasting; nothing tested for cosmetic weight gain.
note: Prescription drug with thromboembolic, hormonal and adrenal-suppression risks; contraindicated in pregnancy.
currentQuick:
Megestrol acetate is a prescription progestin used for advanced breast and endometrial cancer and for anorexia or wasting in people with AIDS. It stimulates appetite and is sometimes mentioned as a weight-gain drug.
All of its published weight-gain evidence comes from sick populations such as people with cancer or HIV. Reviews describe limited and low-quality evidence in elderly patients, and no trials have tested it in healthy people seeking cosmetic weight gain.
How it works: It activates progesterone receptors, suppresses gonadotropins and has some glucocorticoid activity. How it raises appetite is not fully understood; proposed routes include neuropeptide Y, reduced inflammatory cytokines and IGF-1.
Risks and caveats: Documented risks include fluid retention, blood clots, adrenal suppression, lowered sex hormones, bone loss and fetal harm. It is prescription-only in the US and most countries, and the manufacturer of its branded suspension settled a 2013 lawsuit over off-label promotion.
deepLead:
Megestrol acetate is a synthetic progestin, a laboratory-made relative of the hormone progesterone, sold mainly under the brand name Megace. It is a prescription drug used to treat advanced breast and endometrial cancer and, in an oral suspension form, anorexia, cachexia or unexplained significant weight loss in people with AIDS . Its appetite-stimulating effect is the reason it appears in discussions of weight gain.
In appearance-focused settings the drug is relevant only as an appetite stimulant, a category of medicines some people consider when trying to gain weight. Published trials of megestrol for weight gain have been conducted in people with cancer cachexia and HIV-related wasting, not in healthy people seeking cosmetic change. A reference summary notes that studies in elderly patients with weight loss are limited and mostly show little or no weight gain .
Documented adverse effects include fluid retention, vaginal bleeding, thromboembolic events, adrenal suppression with glucocorticoid-like effects, and suppression of sex hormones; it is contraindicated in pregnancy .

name: Cyproheptadine

angle.text: Users take cyproheptadine to boost appetite and eat more while bulking or gaining weight, and some forum posts stack it with pregnenolone and clonidine for stress. Appetite gain is documented, mainly in children; cosmetic weight gain has not been studied.

summary: An allergy antihistamine prescribed off-label for appetite in children; never tested for cosmetic weight gain.
note: Sedating and anticholinergic; overdose is dangerous in children. Rx in US and Canada, OTC in the UK.
currentQuick:
Cyproheptadine is an older antihistamine approved for allergies. Because it also blocks serotonin receptors, it increases appetite, and doctors sometimes prescribe it off-label to underweight children.
In appearance forums it comes up as a weight-gain aid and in supplement-stack discussions. No trial has tested it in healthy adults for cosmetic purposes.
How it works: It blocks histamine H1 and serotonin 5-HT2 receptors and also has anticholinergic and sedating effects. Its appetite effect is attributed to blocking serotonin signalling, though the mechanism is not fully settled.
Risks and caveats: Common effects are drowsiness, dizziness and dry mouth. Rare liver and blood problems are reported, and overdose in children can cause convulsions and death. It is prescription-only in the US and Canada and over the counter in the UK.
deepLead:
Cyproheptadine is a first-generation antihistamine that also blocks serotonin 5-HT2 receptors and has anticholinergic and sedating effects. It is approved for allergic conditions such as seasonal and perennial rhinitis, allergic conjunctivitis and urticaria . Increased appetite and weight gain are recognised effects of the drug, and it is prescribed off-label as an appetite stimulant, particularly in children with poor weight gain .
In appearance communities it is discussed mainly as a weight-gain aid, a category the wiki files under muscle. No published trial has tested it for cosmetic or bodybuilding goals in healthy adults. Trial registrations exist for its use against weight loss in children with cancer and in feeding disorders .
Reported adverse effects include sedation, dizziness, anticholinergic effects such as dry mouth and urinary retention, and, rarely, liver injury and blood disorders. The US label warns about overdose in children .

name: Methylphenidate

angle.text: Appetite loss is a documented effect of methylphenidate, so some users take it to eat less and lean out, or to focus better. It is an ADHD stimulant; its use as a weight-loss aid has not been tested.

summary: An ADHD stimulant whose appetite loss is a documented side effect; never tested as a weight-loss aid.
note: Controlled substance with a boxed warning for abuse, misuse and addiction.
currentQuick:
Methylphenidate is a prescription stimulant for ADHD and narcolepsy. Reduced appetite and weight loss are among its most common side effects, which is why it is sometimes mentioned in weight-control discussions.
It has not been tested as a weight-loss treatment in healthy people, and its use is regulated as a controlled substance.
How it works: It blocks reuptake of dopamine and norepinephrine, raising their levels in the brain. The exact basis of its therapeutic action in ADHD is not established.
Risks and caveats: The US label carries a boxed warning for abuse, misuse and addiction. Other documented effects include insomnia, anxiety, raised heart rate and blood pressure, rare psychiatric events and reduced growth in children. It is Schedule II in the US and Class B in the UK.
deepLead:
Methylphenidate, sold as Ritalin, Concerta and under many other brands, is a central nervous system stimulant prescribed mainly for attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and narcolepsy . It is a controlled substance in most countries, including Schedule II in the US and Class B in the UK .
Its relevance to appearance communities is as an appetite suppressant: loss of appetite and weight loss are among its most common side effects, and some people who obtain stimulants discuss them as aids to eating less. No trial has tested methylphenidate as a weight-loss or cosmetic treatment in healthy people; its weight effects are documented as adverse effects in ADHD patients .
The US label carries a boxed warning for abuse, misuse and addiction, and lists cardiovascular, psychiatric and blood-pressure precautions .

name: Amphetamine / Adderall

angle.text: Forum posters use prescription stimulants to suppress appetite and lose weight, and some claim they improve social ease and gym performance. Appetite suppression is a documented side effect; weight loss and appearance outcomes were not the studied purpose.

summary: A controlled stimulant that suppresses appetite as a side effect; nothing tested for weight loss or looks.
note: Schedule II controlled drug with abuse, cardiovascular and psychiatric risks; unprescribed pills may not be what they claim.
currentQuick:
Adderall is a prescription mixed amphetamine product for ADHD and narcolepsy. Reduced appetite and weight loss are common effects, so some looksmaxxing forum users discuss it for appetite control as well as focus.
No trial has tested it for weight loss in healthy people, and it is a tightly controlled drug in most countries.
How it works: Amphetamines raise dopamine and norepinephrine signalling by promoting release of these neurotransmitters. Dextroamphetamine is the more potent stimulant component of the mixture.
Risks and caveats: Documented effects include higher heart rate and blood pressure, insomnia, anxiety, psychosis at heavy use, and dependence with withdrawal. It is Schedule II in the US, Class B in the UK and Schedule I in Canada. Forum users themselves warn that unprescribed pills may be other substances.
deepLead:
Adderall is a prescription mixed-salts amphetamine product containing roughly equal parts of amphetamine aspartate, amphetamine sulfate, dextroamphetamine saccharate and dextroamphetamine sulfate, used mainly for ADHD and narcolepsy . It is a controlled substance, Schedule II in the US and Class B in the UK .
Loss of appetite and weight loss are common effects, and the drug is listed among appetite suppressants . On looksmax.org, users discuss it for focus, appetite control, social disinhibition and gym use, and the forum also discusses obtaining it without a prescription . No published trial has tested Adderall as a weight-loss or appearance treatment in healthy people.
Documented risks include cardiovascular effects, insomnia, anxiety, psychosis at heavy use, and addiction; surveys show non-medical use is common among US college students .

name: Lisdexamfetamine (Vyvanse)

angle.text: Vyvanse is discussed for its appetite-reducing effect, and it is approved for binge-eating disorder as well as ADHD. Users interested in leaning out cite that effect; weight loss for appearance has not been the studied purpose.

summary: A prodrug of dextroamphetamine approved for ADHD and binge-eating disorder; its link to appearance is appetite and weight, and it is a Schedule II controlled stimulant.
note: Boxed warning for abuse, misuse and addiction; not indicated for weight loss.
currentQuick:
Lisdexamfetamine is a prescription stimulant sold as Vyvanse in the US and Elvanse in Europe. It is approved to treat ADHD in people aged 6 and over and moderate to severe binge-eating disorder (BED) in adults.
Its relevance to appearance culture comes from the BED indication and the appetite-suppressing effects of amphetamines in general. Trials in BED measured binge-eating days, not body weight as a cosmetic goal, and the US label states it is not indicated for weight loss.
How it works: The drug is inactive until red blood cells split off its lysine component, releasing dextroamphetamine. Dextroamphetamine raises norepinephrine and dopamine signalling. The US label says the exact way it works in ADHD and BED is not known.
Risks and caveats: It is a Schedule II controlled substance in the US with a boxed warning for abuse, misuse and addiction. The label also warns of cardiovascular risks, raised blood pressure and heart rate, and psychiatric reactions such as mania or psychosis, and it is contraindicated with MAO inhibitors. It requires a prescription.
deepLead:
Lisdexamfetamine dimesylate, marketed as Vyvanse in the United States and Elvanse in Europe, is a central nervous system stimulant and a prodrug of dextroamphetamine. It is formed by attaching the amino acid lysine to dextroamphetamine, and the active drug is released after enzymatic hydrolysis in the bloodstream . It is prescribed for attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) in children aged 6 and older and adults, and for moderate to severe binge-eating disorder (BED) in adults .
Lisdexamfetamine appears in appearance-related discussion because of its use in BED and because amphetamines reduce appetite. Controlled trials have tested it as a treatment for BED, with reduction in binge-eating days as the main outcome . The US drug label does not list weight loss as an indication .
The drug carries a boxed warning in the US for abuse, misuse and addiction . Systematic reviews of ADHD medications have compared amphetamines including lisdexamfetamine with other drug classes for efficacy and tolerability . No published trial has tested it for cosmetic or looksmaxxing goals.

name: Quinine skin bleaching

angle.text: Quinine appears in reports of unregulated skin-lightening products, where users sought a lighter complexion. It is an antimalarial and tonic-water flavoring; its lightening effect is a claim with no supporting research.

summary: Quinine appears in reports of unregulated skin-lightening products, but no research supports it as a lightening agent and its documented effects are those of an antimalarial drug.
note: Documented only as an ingredient reported in some illicit lightening products; quinine itself is a prescription drug with serious adverse effects.
currentQuick:
Quinine is a bitter alkaloid from cinchona bark, best known as an antimalarial drug and as a flavouring in tonic water. Wikipedia's skin-lightening article mentions that, in a 1997 Paris trafficking case, some users turned to products containing corticosteroids or quinine alongside mercury- or bleach-based preparations.
The sources reviewed contain no studies of quinine for skin lightening, and standard references on quinine do not describe a cosmetic use.
How it works: No lightening mechanism is described in the sources. Quinine's established action is against malaria parasites, where it is thought to interfere with their handling of heme.
Risks and caveats: Quinine at therapeutic levels can cause cinchonism (ringing in the ears, headache, nausea, vision changes) and, rarely, serious blood and heart-rhythm problems. It is prescription-only in the US, UK, Canada and Australia. Unregulated lightening products have been reported to contain other hazardous agents such as mercury and potent steroids.
deepLead:
Quinine is a cinchona alkaloid, first isolated from cinchona bark in 1820, used to treat malaria and as a bitter flavouring in tonic water . Its appearance-related interest comes from a passing mention in descriptions of unregulated skin-lightening products: Wikipedia reports that in a 1997 trafficking case in Paris, users of lightening products used preparations containing corticosteroids or quinine, as well as mercury- or bleach-based ones .
No clinical studies of quinine as a skin-lightening agent were found, and the sources reviewed do not describe a cosmetic mechanism. Clinical literature on quinine concerns malaria and related uses .

name: Ascorbyl glucoside

angle.text: Ascorbyl glucoside is a stabilised vitamin C derivative used in serums to brighten skin, even tone and slow visible aging. Studies on vitamin C support these aims generally, while research on this specific derivative is small.

summary: A stabilised vitamin C derivative used in brightening and anti-ageing skincare, with a small evidence base specific to the ingredient itself.
note: Efficacy data for this specific derivative are sparse; most vitamin C evidence concerns other forms.
currentQuick:
Ascorbyl glucoside is vitamin C (ascorbic acid) with a glucose unit attached, a modification made to make the molecule more stable in skincare formulas. It appears in serums and creams marketed for brightening, evening skin tone and general anti-ageing.
Published human data specific to it are limited. A small case series used an ascorbyl glucoside preparation together with iontophoresis in melasma and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, and it is listed among whitening ingredients in cosmetic analysis papers.
How it works: It is described as a precursor that releases ascorbic acid in the skin. Wikipedia notes that the rate at which it converts to ascorbic acid is unknown, and that it is credited with better stability and penetration than ascorbyl phosphate salts.
Risks and caveats: No specific safety problems are described in the sources reviewed. It is sold as a cosmetic ingredient, and like other topical products it can be tolerated differently by different people.
deepLead:
Ascorbyl glucoside (also written AA-2G; chemical name L-ascorbic acid 2-O-alpha-glucoside) is a derivative of ascorbic acid in which a glucose unit is attached to the vitamin C molecule. It is commonly used in cosmetic products as a way of delivering vitamin C to the skin .
In skincare it is marketed for brightening, evening skin tone and reducing the look of pigmentation, and it appears in cosmetic analytical studies alongside other whitening ingredients such as kojic acid and niacinamide . Skincare communities discuss it as a gentler or more stable alternative to pure ascorbic acid.
Evidence specific to ascorbyl glucoside is limited. One small uncontrolled study in melasma and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation used a proprietary ascorbyl glucoside preparation combined with a device and acid regimen, which makes it hard to attribute any effect to the ingredient alone . Wikipedia notes that clinical efficacy data for its use in skin whitening are not given in its source material, and that its rate of conversion to ascorbic acid in the body is unknown .

name: Cetyl tranexamate mesylate

angle.text: Cetyl tranexamate mesylate is placed in serums aimed at dark spots and uneven tone, as a topical form of tranexamic acid. Evidence consists of early cosmetic-grade data with little independent testing.

summary: A fat-soluble tranexamic acid ester put in serums for dark spots; early cosmetic-grade data, little independent testing.
note: Evidence is mostly small, manufacturer-linked studies.
currentQuick:
Cetyl tranexamate mesylate is a modified form of tranexamic acid designed for skincare. It appears in products aimed at hyperpigmentation, dark spots and post-acne marks.
Published human data are limited to a 2021 cosmetic-dermatology study and a small registered acne-hyperpigmentation trial; no large independent randomised trials were found.
How it works: Tranexamic acid is thought to reduce signalling that drives melanocyte pigment production. The cetyl chain makes the molecule more fat-soluble, intended to help it cross the skin barrier better than the parent compound.
Risks and caveats: Sources reviewed report no specific safety concerns, but long-term data are lacking. It is sold as a cosmetic ingredient; as with any topical, irritation is possible.
deepLead:
Cetyl tranexamate mesylate is a lipophilic derivative of tranexamic acid, formulated as a cosmetic ingredient for topical skin-lightening and hyperpigmentation products. It is the cetyl ester of tranexamic acid supplied as a mesylate salt.
Tranexamic acid itself is a hydrophilic zwitterionic molecule that is described as penetrating the stratum corneum poorly; formulators have used penetration enhancers, microneedling or lipophilic derivatives such as cetyl tranexamate mesylate to address this. The derivative is marketed for uneven skin tone and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation.
Published evidence is limited. A 2021 study in the Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology examined its safety and skin-lightening performance on sun-damaged skin, and a small registered trial examined its effect on acne-related hyperpigmentation.

name: Piroctone olamine

angle.text: Piroctone olamine is used in anti-dandruff shampoos to clear flakes and keep the scalp healthy so hair looks cleaner. It has been compared head-to-head with zinc pyrithione for dandruff; it is a scalp-health ingredient, not studied for hair growth.

summary: A mild antifungal shampoo active for dandruff, tested head-to-head against zinc pyrithione; a scalp-health ingredient, not a hair-growth one.
note: Evidence is for dandruff, not hair growth.
currentQuick:
Piroctone olamine is an antifungal ingredient in many anti-dandruff shampoos. It targets the Malassezia yeasts linked to flaking and itch.
Studies have compared it with zinc pyrithione and ketoconazole shampoos for dandruff and shedding; it is a scalp-condition ingredient rather than a hair-growth treatment.
How it works: It is thought to enter fungal cells and bind iron, disrupting energy production; the exact mechanism is not fully established.
Risks and caveats: EU rules cap it at 1.0% in rinse-off and 0.5% in other cosmetics. Labels advise avoiding eyes and stopping use if irritation or allergy occurs.
deepLead:
Piroctone olamine is the ethanolamine salt of piroctone, a hydroxypyridone-type antifungal used mainly in anti-dandruff shampoos and scalp-care products. It is sold by Clariant as Octopirox.
It is aimed at Malassezia yeasts associated with dandruff and seborrheic dermatitis. Several comparative trials have tested piroctone olamine shampoos against zinc pyrithione shampoos. In the EU it is permitted as a cosmetic ingredient up to 1.0% in rinse-off and 0.5% in other products.

name: Zinc pyrithione

angle.text: Zinc pyrithione is the classic active in dandruff shampoos, used to clear flakes and calm seborrheic dermatitis for a cleaner-looking scalp and hair. It is well studied for dandruff; it is not promoted for hair growth.

summary: The classic dandruff-shampoo antifungal; long used OTC in the US but barred from EU cosmetics since 2021.
note: Evidence is for dandruff; regulatory status differs between US and EU.
currentQuick:
Zinc pyrithione is the active in many dandruff shampoos. It acts against the yeasts linked to flaking and scalp itch.
It is a standard comparator in dandruff trials. It is not a hair-growth treatment.
How it works: It is thought to disrupt fungal membrane transport and raise intracellular copper, damaging iron-sulfur proteins.
Risks and caveats: US labels warn against use on damaged skin or in young children. The EU classifies it as a reproductive toxicant and has barred it in cosmetics since 2021; it is also toxic to aquatic life as an antifouling agent.
deepLead:
Zinc pyrithione (pyrithione zinc, ZPT) is a zinc coordination complex with antifungal and antibacterial properties. It is the active ingredient in many anti-dandruff shampoos and body washes and is used for seborrheic dermatitis; it is also used in antifouling paints and some textiles.
It has been used in dandruff products for decades and is approved as an over-the-counter dandruff ingredient in the US. Its regulatory status differs by region: Wikipedia reports that the EU has barred its use in cosmetics since December 2021, citing a reproductive-toxicity classification and environmental concerns.

name: Selenium disulfide

angle.text: Selenium disulfide shampoos such as Selsun Blue are used to clear dandruff and scalp scaling for a cleaner look. It is studied for scalp conditions, and hair growth is not its documented use.

summary: An old-school dandruff shampoo active (Selsun Blue); a scalp-condition treatment, not a hair-growth one.
note: Can stain light hair and jewellery; avoid damaged skin per labels.
currentQuick:
Selenium disulfide is an antifungal and keratolytic ingredient in dandruff shampoos such as Selsun Blue. It is used for dandruff, scalp seborrheic dermatitis and tinea versicolor.
It is generally regarded as a second option after ketoconazole for seborrheic dermatitis.
How it works: It acts as an antifungal against Malassezia and loosens scale as a keratolytic; the detailed molecular mechanism is not well described.
Risks and caveats: Scalp itching, burning, hair lightening, orange staining and discolouration of jewellery are reported. Absorption is higher through damaged skin. Strength limits differ by country.
deepLead:
Selenium disulfide (selenium sulfide) is a topical antifungal and keratolytic agent used in shampoos for dandruff, scalp seborrheic dermatitis and tinea versicolor. It is better described as a mixture of selenium sulfide ring compounds than a single pure compound.
It entered US medical use in 1951 and is on the WHO Essential Medicines List. The best-known OTC product is Selsun Blue (1% selenium disulfide). It is not first-line therapy for seborrheic dermatitis, with ketoconazole generally tried earlier.

name: Erythrulose

angle.text: Erythrulose is a sugar used with DHA in self-tanners to give a sunless tan, a color change visible within hours. It tends to develop more slowly and fade more evenly in cosmetic-industry descriptions; independent trials were not found.

summary: A raspberry-derived sugar used alongside DHA in self-tanners; claims rest on cosmetic-industry descriptions, with no trials found.
note: No published clinical studies of tanning performance found.
currentQuick:
Erythrulose is a small sugar used in sunless tanning products, usually together with DHA. It is described as giving a gradual, bronze-toned colour.
No clinical studies of its tanning effect were found.
How it works: It is described as reacting with amino acids in the outer skin layer (a Maillard-type reaction) to form brown pigments, more slowly than DHA.
Risks and caveats: The sources reviewed contain no safety or regulatory data specific to erythrulose.
deepLead:
Erythrulose is a four-carbon ketose sugar (a tetrose) found naturally in fruits such as raspberries and used in cosmetics as a sunless tanning ingredient. It is usually produced by microbial fermentation.
As a tanning agent it is described as reacting with amino acids in the outer skin layer in a Maillard-type reaction to give a gradual brown colour, and it is commonly combined with dihydroxyacetone (DHA) in self-tanners to affect colour development and evenness. No clinical trials of its tanning performance were found in the sources reviewed.

name: Silymarin (milk thistle)

angle.text: Silymarin is a milk thistle liver supplement that some users take for its antioxidant chemistry, hoping for clearer skin or slower visible aging. The skin and appearance role is theoretical and has not been tested.

summary: A milk thistle liver supplement with antioxidant chemistry; any skin or appearance role is theoretical.
note: Appearance use is untested; possible drug interactions.
currentQuick:
Silymarin is the active extract of milk thistle, mainly sold for liver support. Its connection to appearance is limited to proposed antioxidant and skin-protective effects.
No human trials for skin or cosmetic outcomes were found.
How it works: It is described as scavenging free radicals and chelating metals, with anti-inflammatory effects.
Risks and caveats: It may inhibit drug-metabolising enzymes and transporters, so drug interactions cannot be excluded; pregnancy data are limited.
deepLead:
Silymarin is a standardised extract of milk thistle (Silybum marianum) containing flavonolignans, chiefly silibinin (silybin), along with silychristin and silidianin. It is used mainly as a liver-support supplement and has been studied for antioxidant activity.
Its relevance to appearance is indirect. Wikipedia notes proposed skin benefits such as protection from UV damage and inflammation, but reports no human clinical trials for skin or cosmetic use.

name: Vilon

angle.text: Vilon is a Lys-Glu dipeptide from Khavinson's Russian peptide bioregulator program, discussed in longevity circles as an anti-aging candidate. Data come from mouse and cell studies; no human trials or appearance link is known.

summary: A lab-studied Lys-Glu dipeptide from Russian gerontology research; mouse and cell data only, no human trials and no known link to appearance.
note: Research peptide; not an approved medicine, and its claims rest largely on one research group.
currentQuick:
Vilon is a two-amino-acid peptide (lysine and glutamic acid) developed by Vladimir Khavinson's group in St. Petersburg. It is described as an immune-system and anti-aging "bioregulator".
The published work is mostly cell-culture and mouse experiments, much of it from the originating institute. No controlled human trial of Vilon itself was found, and it has no established effect on appearance.
How it works: Khavinson's group proposes that Vilon loosens condensed chromatin in ageing lymphocytes and so reactivates silenced genes. This is reported from cell cultures and has not been shown in humans [1].
Risks and caveats: No systematic human safety data were found. It is not an approved drug in the US or EU and is sold as a research peptide.
deepLead:
Vilon is a synthetic dipeptide made of the amino acids lysine and glutamic acid (Lys-Glu). It was developed by the Russian gerontologist Vladimir Khavinson and colleagues at the St. Petersburg Institute of Bioregulation and Gerontology as part of a program on short peptide "bioregulators" . It is described as an immunomodulatory and geroprotective (anti-aging) candidate.
Published work on Vilon consists mainly of cell-culture and animal experiments, much of it from Khavinson's own group. Reported findings include effects on lymphocyte chromatin and on tumour development and lifespan in mice . No controlled human trial of Vilon specifically was found, and it is not an approved medicine in the US or EU. It has no established link to facial appearance; its place in looksmaxxing discussion is as a longevity peptide.

name: Pinealon

angle.text: Pinealon is a short peptide marketed for brain and anti-aging use in nootropic and longevity communities, with a looks angle drawn via sleep and healthy aging. Evidence is cell and rat data plus small Russian-language human reports.

summary: A Glu-Asp-Arg tripeptide from Khavinson's lab marketed for brain and anti-aging use; cell and rat data, only small Russian-language human reports.
note: Research peptide; not approved, and evidence is largely from one research network.
currentQuick:
Pinealon is a three-amino-acid peptide (glutamic acid, aspartic acid, arginine) developed in Russia as a brain-focused "bioregulator". It is promoted for neuroprotection and anti-aging.
Studies are mostly cell cultures and rats. A few Russian-language reports involve human groups, but details and independent replication are lacking.
How it works: Lab studies report that pinealon reduces reactive-oxygen-species build-up in cultured neurons and other cells and modulates signalling such as ERK 1/2 [1]. Labelled short peptides, including pinealon, were also reported to enter the cell nucleus and bind DNA in vitro [2].
Risks and caveats: No systematic safety data are available. It is not an approved medicine and is sold as a research peptide.
deepLead:
Pinealon is a synthetic tripeptide with the sequence Glu-Asp-Arg (EDR) developed in Vladimir Khavinson's peptide bioregulator program. It is described as acting on the brain and nervous system, and it is discussed in nootropic and anti-aging circles.
Published research consists of cell-culture studies and rat experiments, such as protection of rat offspring from prenatal hyperhomocysteinemia  and reduced oxidative stress in cultured cells . Russian-language reports describe human groups . It is not an approved drug, and no link to facial appearance is documented.

name: Thymogen

angle.text: Thymogen is an immunomodulator dipeptide from Russian peptide research, discussed in longevity circles for its immune and anti-aging claims. Evidence is mostly animal and cell data with thin human reports; no appearance use is documented.

summary: A Glu-Trp dipeptide immunomodulator derived from the calf-thymus extract Thymalin; Russian drug lineage, animal and cell data, thin human evidence.
note: Described in the literature as a pharmaceutical; not approved in the US or EU as far as sources show, and evidence is largely from one research network.
currentQuick:
Thymogen is the brand name of a synthetic dipeptide, glutamyl-tryptophan, isolated from the calf thymus preparation Thymalin and then made synthetically. It is described as an immune system modulator.
Research is mostly animal and cell work from Khavinson's group; one rat study reported slower ageing and fewer spontaneous tumours. It has no documented appearance use.
How it works: Reported to activate T-cell differentiation, alter intracellular cyclic nucleotides and activate neutrophil chemotaxis [1]. It has also been grouped among interferon-inducing immunomodulators developed in former socialist countries [2].
Risks and caveats: No systematic safety data in the sources; it is not approved in the US or EU.

Thymogen is the brand name of a pharmaceutical based on the synthetic dipeptide L-Glu-L-Trp, which Khavinson's group isolated from the calf thymus extract Thymalin and then synthesised . It is characterised as an immunomodulator.
Reported studies include a rat experiment in which the dipeptide was associated with slower ageing and inhibition of spontaneous carcinogenesis , and cell-culture work comparing it with other Khavinson peptides . A review places it among interferon-inducing immunomodulators developed mainly in former socialist countries and little known in the West . No link to appearance is documented.

name: Bronchogen

angle.text: Bronchogen is a short peptide from Khavinson's bioregulator program aimed at lung tissue, discussed in longevity circles as an organ-specific anti-aging peptide. Data are rat and cell studies only; no human trials and no appearance link.

summary: An Ala-Glu-Asp-Leu tetrapeptide from Khavinson's lab aimed at lung tissue; rat and cell studies only, no human trials, no appearance link.
note: Research peptide; evidence is preclinical and mostly from one research group.
currentQuick:
Bronchogen is a four-amino-acid peptide (Ala-Glu-Asp-Leu) from the Khavinson bioregulator program, described as targeting bronchial and lung tissue.
Published studies are in rats and cell cultures; no human trial was found, and it has no documented appearance use.
How it works: Reported to stimulate differentiation markers in aged bronchial cell cultures [1] and, in rats with an induced obstructive lung condition, to improve bronchial epithelium and reduce inflammation [2][3]. A biophysical study reported it stabilises DNA against melting [4].
Risks and caveats: No human safety data; not an approved medicine.
deepLead:
Bronchogen is a synthetic tetrapeptide (Ala-Glu-Asp-Leu, AEDL) developed within Vladimir Khavinson's program on short peptide bioregulators and described as directed at bronchial and lung tissue .
Evidence is preclinical. Studies report that it stimulated differentiation markers in aged human bronchial cell cultures  and, in rats with obstructive lung pathology, modulated bronchial epithelium and inflammation . No human trial is known, and no connection to appearance is documented.

name: Cardiogen

angle.text: Cardiogen is a short peptide from Khavinson's bioregulator program aimed at heart tissue, discussed in longevity circles as an anti-aging peptide. Data are sparse rat and cell studies with no human trials; no appearance link is known.

summary: An Ala-Glu-Asp-Arg tetrapeptide from Khavinson's lab aimed at heart tissue; sparse rat and cell data, no human trials.
note: Research peptide; extremely thin evidence base.
currentQuick:
Cardiogen is a four-amino-acid peptide (Ala-Glu-Asp-Arg) from the Khavinson bioregulator program, described as acting on cardiovascular tissue.
The literature is thin: cell and rat experiments only, and no human studies. It has no documented appearance use.
How it works: Reported to stimulate proliferation in heart-tissue cultures and lower the pro-apoptotic protein p53, and to interact with DNA and histones [1].
Risks and caveats: In a rat transplanted-sarcoma model it was reported to inhibit tumour growth [2]; no human safety data exist, and it is not an approved medicine.
deepLead:
Cardiogen is a synthetic tetrapeptide, Ala-Glu-Asp-Arg (AEDR), developed in the Khavinson research program and described as a cardiovascular-targeted bioregulator .
Reported work is limited to organotypic cultures and rats, including stimulation of proliferation in heart explants  and dose-dependent inhibition of transplanted M-1 sarcoma growth in old rats . It is not approved for therapeutic use and has no documented relationship to appearance.
